learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: `n` bulbs are all off. In round 1 you toggle every bulb, in round 2 every 2nd bulb, in round 3 every 3rd bulb, and so on until round `n`. **How many bulbs are on** at the end?

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- Does round r toggle bulbs r, 2r, 3r…? (Yes.)
- How large is n? (Up to int.MaxValue — simulation is impossible.)
- n = 0? (0.)

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: Bulb i changes once for every r that divides i. Divisors come in pairs (d and i/d) — except when d = i/d, which only happens for perfect squares. An odd number of toggles leaves a bulb on, so exactly the perfect squares stay on.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md: I would say, before coding: "B."ulb i is toggled once per divisor of i; divisors pair up except for perfect squares, so the bulbs left on are exactly the perfect squares — the answer is floor(√n), O(1)."

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md: Bulb i changes once for every r that divides i. Divisors come in pairs (d and i/d) — except when d = i/d, which only happens for perfect squares. An odd number of toggles leaves a bulb on, so exactly the perfect squares stay on.

learn.title: 11 · AI usage strategy
learn.md:
- Make the design decision yourself, then ask the assistant to attack it.
- Delegate the mechanical parts only after the structure is fixed.

**Prompts for this question:**

- *Check my design — no code* — "I believe bulb i is toggled once per divisor of i; divisors pair up except for perfect squares, so the bulbs left on are exactly the perfect squares — the answer is floor(√n), O(1). Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?"
- *Review, do not rewrite* — "Review my implementation for correctness and edge cases. Do not rewrite the code. List problems most severe first, each with the input that triggers it."
- *Race conditions* — "Now review this implementation for race conditions if multiple threads call OnAfter concurrently. For each race, give the interleaving that breaks it. Then name the smallest synchronization boundary that preserves correctness. Do not write code yet."
- *Tests that expose bugs* — "Suggest tests that could expose bugs in my implementation: boundaries, duplicates, empty and invalid input, and concurrency where it applies. For each, say why the expected value is correct."
- *Complexity check* — "What is the time and space complexity of each public method as written? Do not claim a bound unless every step achieves it."
- *Requirement change* — "The requirement changed: Add BulbSwitcher.OnBulbs(n): the 1-based positions of the bulbs that are on, ascending. List which members need to change and which do not, before writing any code."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- Simulating n rounds — O(n log n) at best, impossible for n = 10⁹.
- (int)Math.Sqrt(n) without checking — floating-point can be off by one for large n.
- Thinking only primes stay on.

learn.title: 14 · Scalability considerations
learn.md:
**Level 4 — Scale**

- *Only rounds 1..m, with m < n.* — Then bulb i's toggles = divisors of i that are ≤ m — no closed form; count with a sieve up to n.
